title: Navigation Guards
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Navigation Guards in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Navigation Guards within Vue Router and Application Navigation. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Routing lets a Vue app behave like a multi-page product while remaining a single-page application in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Navigation Guards: URL-driven navigation
content_blocks.alt_text: URL-driven navigation diagram for lesson 76: Navigation Guards. Represent addressable navigation in the route → Resolve route parameters and navigation policy → Render the matching route component
content_blocks.caption: Routing flow: the URL determines the matched view; frontend guards improve navigation but do not secure backend APIs.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue Router maps URLs to views and supports dynamic parameters, nested layouts, guards, lazy-loaded components, and navigation state. This lesson focuses on Navigation Guards. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Global guards
items.text: For Global guards, keep the URL as the addressable navigation state, use named route records when practical, and handle invalid parameters or failed navigation explicitly. A route guard improves navigation flow but does not replace backend access control.

content_blocks.expected_output: A navigation to a route marked requiresAuth redirects to login if the UI auth state says no; this is not a substitute for server-side authorization.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This excerpt belongs after router and auth store setup. Validate permissions on protected API routes regardless of client navigation.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Navigation Guards with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Per-route guards”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember: Vue Router maps URLs to views and supports dynamic parameters, nested layouts, guards, lazy-loaded components, and navigation state. For Navigation Guards, keep the example small, verify the rendered or logged result, and consult the official references when behavior depends on a specific Vue or ecosystem version.

content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Navigation Guards” that applies “Global guards”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Global guards”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Navigation Guards belongs to the broader area Vue Router and Application Navigation.
The main concept to practice is Global guards.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
